definition: The distinctive, earthy scent produced when rain falls on dry ground, caused chiefly by an oil exuded by certain plants during drought and by the compound geosmin released from soil bacteria.
etymology: Coined in 1964 by Australian mineralogists Isabel Joy Bear and R. G. Thomas, who built it from the Greek petra, meaning stone or rock, and ichor, the rarefied fluid said to flow through the veins of the gods in place of blood. So the word captures something humble and something divine at once: the blood of the gods seeping up through ordinary stone.
usage: After weeks of dry November air, the petrichor that rose from the garden path when the first real rain came was almost narcotic, stopping her mid-stride with its insistence on being noticed.
